home.eyebrow: ROUGH AS GUTS • GUIDES IN DEVELOPMENT
home.title: For someone you love. Who drives you bloody nuts.
home.lead: Funny picture guides for the habits that make families, mates and co-workers say, “How have you survived this long?”
home.heroAlt: A lively Australian comic scene with several adults discovering a Rough as Guts guide among the everyday mess they have created.
home.intro: Buy it for a mate. Give it to your partner. Leave it on the kitchen bench and let nature take its course. Rough as Guts is being developed around a simple idea: a good laugh can get a useful thought through the door.

sections.heading: The present with a fairly obvious hint
sections.body: Some gifts say, “I was thinking of you.” This one might say, “I was thinking of your wet towel, your seventh abandoned coffee mug and the way you pack for a weekend like you’re fleeing the country.” The affection stays. The habit gets a proper roasting.
bullets: For family members whose contribution to the washing-up is a weather report.
For mates who treat preparation as a personal insult.
For co-workers with a PhD in making a five-minute job take all afternoon.
For yourself, when the picture looks uncomfortably familiar.

sections.heading: A whole crew of rough edges
sections.body: Men’s and women’s editions are in development, alongside Young Crew material and workplace ideas. Different people, different situations, plenty of room for everyone to recognise themselves. The joke can follow a character, a couple, a household or an entire camp.
bullets: Men: borrowed tools, five-minute repairs, mystery leftovers and sideline experts.
Women: handbag archaeology, epic voice notes, op-shop rescues and feral departures.
Young Crew: growing independence with humour and practical little wins.
Worksites: shared facilities, camp life and visual support for reviewed task material.

sections.heading: Five new directions. All in development.
sections.body: The original mine-and-camp material is a starting point. These proposed topics take the same humour into the rest of life.
bullets: Dating and getting along: listening, manners, boundaries and reading the room.
Exercise: starting sensibly, learning the movement and showing up again.
Cooking, cleaning and hygiene: feeding yourself and leaving somewhere fit for other humans.
Parenting: being present, sharing the work and remembering the actual child.
Travel: packing, planning and behaving like a decent visitor.

sections.heading: One good idea can go a long way
sections.body: A strong gag could become a book page, poster, small card, short animation or newsletter feature. The useful bit needs to survive each format: a recognisable situation, a clear action and a joke that lands.
bullets: A picture you understand at a glance.
A caption worth reading aloud.
A useful point you can remember tomorrow.
Enough warmth that you might give it to someone you actually like.

sections.heading: Have a rummage
sections.body: The original 45-slide deck is the source archive. The Systems page shows how an observation can become a clearer, funnier illustrated idea. New editions and formats are in development; this site is a place to explore the work as it takes shape.

sample_gags.title: The Museum of Unwashed Mugs
sample_gags.setup: Every room has a different exhibit. Several appear to be developing their own ecosystem.
sample_gags.punchline: The dishwasher has capacity. Your bedside table has tenure.
sample_gags.visual: A mock museum tour through a normal house, with abandoned mugs displayed under tiny spotlights and an unimpressed housemate holding a washing-up brush.

sample_gags.title: Weekend Away. Expedition Equipment.
sample_gags.setup: Three bags, two backup jackets and no toothbrush.
sample_gags.punchline: Excellent. You’re prepared for everything except being there.
sample_gags.visual: Two adults beside an overpacked car; camping gear towers above a small, conspicuously empty toiletries bag.

sample_gags.title: The Five-Minute Job
sample_gags.setup: It began with a loose handle. The whole room is now in pieces.
sample_gags.punchline: The first tool you needed was a pause.
sample_gags.visual: A DIY enthusiast surveys an absurd spread of dismantled household objects while a mate holds a single replacement screw.

men.title: For the bloke who reckons he’s got a system.
men.lead: The five-minute repair, the borrowed tool and the fridge tub nobody will open. There’s a useful hint in here somewhere. Probably under his keys.
men.heroAlt: A puzzled adult man holds a tea towel stiff as a plank beside a sink full of dishes and overflowing laundry.
men.intro: Give it to the mate who returns a drill without the charger. The brother whose leftovers have survived two governments. The partner who says “nearly done” from inside a wall. These proposed chapters give a few familiar habits a proper roasting, with enough affection that he might still lend you the book afterwards.

sections.heading: The Five-Minute Job Needs a Site Office
sections.body: He went in to tighten a cupboard handle. The door is off, the contents are on the floor and he’s explaining why the whole kitchen was badly designed anyway. There are now three hardware receipts and no available bench space. This chapter is for the enthusiastic starter whose family would quite like to see him finish something.
bullets: “While I’m here” is how a loose screw becomes a renovation.
The instruction sheet is currently protecting the bench from his coffee.
He’s saved forty dollars. The household has lost Saturday.
sections.picture_idea: A man stands proudly beside a cupboard stripped into dozens of parts. His partner holds one loose handle, and a tiny site office has appeared at the end of the kitchen bench.

sections.heading: The Fridge Witness Protection Program
sections.body: Every container has a lid. Very few have an explanation. He lifts one, says “still smells alright” and promptly asks if anyone wants takeaway. The comedy lives in the leftovers he keeps out of principle, the sauce bottles with one teaspoon left and the empty milk carton thoughtfully returned to the shelf. A clean-out would answer several household questions.
bullets: “That’s from Tuesday.” Which Tuesday has been referred to the archives.
The good container has been missing since the curry incident.
Putting an empty carton back is a very small act of warfare.
sections.picture_idea: A man peers into a fridge full of identical tubs. Several wear tiny disguises, while a family member holds the missing container’s lid like a detective displaying evidence.

sections.heading: The Apology Has Footnotes
sections.body: He’s sorry, obviously. First he needs twelve minutes to establish the weather, the traffic, the quality of the signage and what his mate would have done. By the time he reaches “but”, everyone has forgotten the original offence. These pages follow the heroic effort involved in saying a simple thing without turning it into an appeal hearing.
bullets: “I’m sorry you took it that way” has arrived wearing a fake moustache.
His explanation now needs a whiteboard and a second witness.
Try “I stuffed that up.” There’s still time to enjoy the afternoon.
sections.picture_idea: Different adults sit around a backyard table while an apologising man presents an absurdly long flowchart. A small card reading “Sorry. My fault.” waits unused beside his elbow.

sections.heading: The Borrowed Drill Has Changed Families
sections.body: A mate lent him a drill for the weekend. It now has a regular parking spot, a preferred shelf and possibly voting rights at his place. Meanwhile the owner has bought another one. This chapter collects the missing chargers, blunt blades and mysterious accessories that make lending a tool feel like sponsoring a very expensive exchange student.
bullets: “Just finishing with it” is entering its third financial year.
He returned the case. A bold opening offer.
A borrowed mower should come home with fewer problems than it left with.
sections.picture_idea: A borrowed drill poses in a framed family photo in a man’s shed. Outside, its original owner waits with an empty case and an increasingly patient expression.

sections.heading: The Sideline Has a New National Coach
sections.body: It’s an under-tens game at the suburban oval or the country rec ground. He’s arrived with tactical concerns normally reserved for a World Cup final. His child is more interested in the orange slices. These pages find the point where enthusiastic support becomes a full broadcast, complete with disputed decisions and an audience trying to watch their own kids.
bullets: The coach has a plan. Apparently Dad has a louder one.
His match analysis lasted longer than the match.
The kid asked for a lift home, not a performance review.
sections.picture_idea: Several parents watch a small junior sports game. One dad has unfolded a giant tactics board beside the esky while his child offers him an orange slice and a quiet seat.

sample_gags.title: The Date Commentary Channel
sample_gags.setup: He has explained his job, his old car, his new car and the correct way to reverse a trailer.
sample_gags.punchline: Strong opening. Now find out her name.
sample_gags.visual: Two adults on a casual date; one man’s speech bubble has become an enormous map of unrelated stories while his date patiently holds a small question mark.

sample_gags.title: Dad Packed the Bag
sample_gags.setup: Drinks, snacks, wipes, hat. He proudly announces everything is ready.
sample_gags.visual: An elaborately prepared parent stands beside a packed day bag while the child waits calmly in the doorway holding the missing shoes.

sample_gags.title: The Gym Opening Ceremony
sample_gags.setup: New shoes. New watch. New bottle. An inspirational announcement.
sample_gags.punchline: Tomorrow’s workout still needs you to turn up.
sample_gags.visual: A man cuts a ceremonial ribbon in front of a single exercise mat while a calendar quietly displays the following day.

women.title: For the woman who calls this “under control”.
women.lead: The handbag excavation, the five-minute voice note and the dog who pre-rinses the dishes. A few rough edges deserve their own illustrated guide.
women.heroAlt: An amused adult woman holds a forgotten leftovers jar wearing a tiny birthday hat in front of an open fridge.
women.intro: For the friend who brings home another “easy restoration”. The sister whose quick message needs an intermission. The partner who arrives looking immaculate and leaves holding her shoes and someone else’s cake. Give her a laugh and a fairly obvious hint. These proposed chapters have plenty of mess, cheek and questionable judgement to go round.

sections.heading: Your Handbag Has Applied for a Mining Lease
sections.body: She can produce pliers, emergency earrings and a cough lolly from a previous decade. Finding the house key requires a full excavation on the café table. Somewhere beneath the useful stuff is a sandwich she has stopped asking questions about. This chapter celebrates being prepared for almost anything, provided nobody needs it within the next twenty minutes.
bullets: She offered you a mint, then blew the handbag fluff off it.
The receipt says 2019. The banana has declined to comment.
Her keys are in the safe place. Unfortunately, so is everything else.
sections.picture_idea: A woman empties an enormous handbag across a small café table. A tiny excavator works through receipts while her friend holds up one key and a remarkably old banana.

sections.heading: That Quick Voice Note Needs an Interval
sections.body: She’s walking through the supermarket or waiting outside the rural post office, recording “one quick thing”. It includes a family dispute, an unrelated dog sighting and every item currently on special. The intended listener only asked which milk to buy. These pages explore the moment a handy message becomes a podcast with accidental public participation.
bullets: The checkout operator is now invested in what happened at Christmas.
“Long story short” was four minutes ago.
Her friend replies, “So, full cream or skim?”
sections.picture_idea: A woman records a voice note beside a supermarket fridge. Her speech bubble winds through several aisles, and the checkout operator holds a tiny interval sign.

sections.heading: The Op-Shop Rescue Has Rescued Your Spare Room
sections.body: A cracked birdbath. A cabinet without handles. A lamp with a plug nobody recognises. She can see the potential, and everybody else can see the trailer filling up. The clean-up, the repairs and the question of where it will live belong to future her. Future her would quite like a word before the next council collection.
bullets: “It only needs a quick sand” has swallowed another long weekend.
She bought a second cabinet to store the bits for the first cabinet.
The bargain was fifteen dollars. Getting the car back in the garage is looking dearer.
sections.picture_idea: A woman beams beside a trailer of dubious second-hand treasures. A family member attempts to reach the garage through a narrow corridor of unfinished rescues.

sections.heading: Five-Star Entrance. Feral Departure.
sections.body: She arrives at the wedding, the races or the bowls-club do looking magnificent. Hours later, the shoes are in a chip box and she’s carrying cake on a raffle ticket. The outfit has survived through determination and one overloaded safety pin. This chapter follows the grand exit of someone who insists she has packed everything she could possibly need.
bullets: The emergency flats are safely at home, having an excellent night.
She’s holding the good shoes like two freshly caught fish.
The clutch fits a lipstick. The evening has required a small removal truck.
sections.picture_idea: A comic triptych shows three different women leaving adult social events: shoes in a chip box, cake balanced on a raffle ticket and an immaculate fascinator above a very improvised outfit repair.

sections.heading: The Dog Is Not the Dishwasher
sections.body: The dog shares the couch, the car seat and increasingly the cutlery. She calls his interest in the roast “helping”, then wipes a licked spoon on her jeans before putting it back. Visitors have begun guarding their plates. These pages give the much-loved family pest a break from his self-appointed job as head of kitchen quality control.
bullets: “He only licked the handle.” A defence nobody requested.
The dog has a seat at dinner and absolutely no qualifications.
She licked the serving spoon. Even the dog looked concerned.
sections.picture_idea: A woman stands beside a dog wearing a tiny kitchen-inspector badge. A guest protects a plate while a proper washing-up brush and sink wait conspicuously in the background.

sample_gags.title: The Chair Has Joined the Wardrobe
sample_gags.setup: Clean clothes. Worn-once clothes. Clothes awaiting a decision.
sample_gags.punchline: At this point, the chair needs its own postcode.
sample_gags.visual: A woman attempts to sit while a towering clothes pile on an ordinary chair has acquired a tiny mailbox and street number.

sample_gags.title: Packing for All Possible Selves
sample_gags.setup: Beach self. Hiking self. Fancy-dinner self. Emergency cold-weather self.
sample_gags.punchline: Current self cannot lift the suitcase.
sample_gags.visual: A traveller stands beside an enormous suitcase; small comic versions of her imagined holiday plans compete to add one more item.

sample_gags.title: The Workout Collection
sample_gags.setup: She has saved enough exercise videos to keep a sports institute busy.
sample_gags.punchline: Pick one. The bookmark button has had a decent workout.
sample_gags.visual: A woman in exercise gear faces a comically long ribbon of saved videos while a single mat and simple timer wait nearby.

youth.title: A few useful clues for doing more of life yourself.
youth.lead: Funny, practical picture guides for the everyday things nobody is born knowing.
youth.heroAlt: A friendly comic group of teenagers helping one another with school bags, a shared kitchen, phones and everyday tasks.
youth.intro: School, friends, home, messages, work experience and getting yourself somewhere on time can pile up quickly. Young Crew is a proposed, school-appropriate part of Rough as Guts, built around situations young people recognise and skills they can actually use.

sections.heading: You can learn this stuff
sections.body: Being unsure is a normal place to begin. A picture can make an awkward moment easier to talk about: an overdue message, a forgotten item, a room that got away from you or a job you have never tried before.
bullets: Show the situation clearly.
Offer a manageable next action.
Leave room to try again.
Keep the person’s dignity intact.

sections.heading: Everyday independence
sections.body: The proposed guides focus on small skills that make a day easier: getting ready, looking after your things, preparing simple food, cleaning up and treating shared spaces with care.
bullets: Check the bag before leaving.
Put an essential item somewhere you can find it.
Learn a simple meal and clean up afterwards.
Keep clothes, sports gear and personal hygiene on the radar.
Ask for help with something unfamiliar.

sections.heading: Friends, messages and finding your words
sections.body: A useful joke can open a conversation about listening, handling disagreement, respecting boundaries or pausing before sending a message. Young Crew material should sound like it understands the situation, with language a young person can use.
bullets: Give people a chance to finish speaking.
Check what someone means before building a whole story around it.
Pause when a reply is coming from anger.
Find a trusted adult when a problem feels too big to carry alone.

sections.heading: Moving, travelling and trying new things
sections.body: Exercise, everyday journeys and work experience offer plenty of visual humour. The proposed pages explore preparation, realistic expectations and how to ask a good question when everyone else seems to know what is happening.
bullets: Know where you are going and how you are getting home.
Bring the essentials for the activity.
Learn a new task from someone who can show you.
Choose an achievable start and build confidence through practice.

sections.heading: Made to read together
sections.body: A parent, teacher, youth worker, coach or young person could use a single page to start an ordinary conversation. The humour needs to work for the reader, with characters who have strengths, make mistakes and get another go.
bullets: School-appropriate language and situations.
Different kinds of young people with a fair share of the good ideas.
Clear pictures with one useful point.
Young Crew concepts are in development and need feedback from young readers and the adults supporting them.

sample_gags.title: The Bag That Was Ready Yesterday
sample_gags.setup: The bag is zipped. The shoes are on. The bus is coming.
sample_gags.punchline: Your lunch has chosen to stay on the bench.
sample_gags.visual: A teenager at the front door points proudly to a packed bag while a lunchbox on the kitchen bench holds a tiny sign saying WAIT.

sample_gags.title: The Sports Bag Wildlife Reserve
sample_gags.setup: Something in the bag has been there since last week.
sample_gags.punchline: Air the gear before it starts charging rent.
sample_gags.visual: Two teenagers open a sports bag; cartoon smell lines form a tiny imaginary creature while one holds a laundry basket.

sample_gags.title: The Reply You Wrote While Furious
sample_gags.setup: A very long message. Several capital letters. A dramatic ending.
sample_gags.punchline: Save the draft. Take a breath. Read it again.
sample_gags.visual: A teenager’s phone displays a comically oversized message bubble while a friend offers a pause button on a small card.

workplace.title: Give them something they’ll actually stop to read.
workplace.lead: Workshop posters, mine camps, shared facilities and the familiar moment when enthusiasm gets ahead of thought.
workplace.heroAlt: An Australian mine-camp noticeboard with bold humorous posters, a crib-room scene and a crew stopping to read together.
workplace.intro: Rough as Guts began with illustrated mine-and-camp ideas. That setting has plenty of material: crib rooms, shared walls, fatigue, traffic, gear, cleaning up and people convinced they can save thirty seconds. The opportunity is to make a useful point memorable and get the details right.

sections.heading: Start with a real situation
sections.body: A good workplace gag needs the grain of something a crew recognises. What keeps happening? What gets misunderstood? What small action would make the job or shared space work better? The source story gives the picture somewhere solid to stand.
bullets: A familiar place and a specific moment.
A behaviour the reader can recognise.
A consequence that makes visual sense.
A better action the reader can identify.

sections.heading: Camp life counts
sections.body: The way people live together matters after the shift finishes too. Noise, bathrooms, laundry, meals, shared screens and cleaning are rich territory for humour with an immediately useful point.
bullets: Quiet around people who are sleeping.
Leaving shared facilities ready for the next person.
Owning the mess you make.
Handling small annoyances before they become camp-wide entertainment.

sections.heading: Choose the format for the job
sections.body: A workshop poster needs to work from a few metres away. Big text, a clear picture and strong contrast help the point land quickly. A pocket card needs a quick point of reference. A booklet has room for examples. A short animation can show timing and consequences that one still picture struggles to explain.
bullets: Posters: one message, a readable picture and a short caption.
Toolbox-talk and newsletter material: one familiar scenario to discuss.
Cards and booklets: concise reminders with room for necessary context.
Manual illustrations: clear scenes tied to reviewed text.
Short animations: a visible action and consequence.

sections.heading: A little humour in the SWMS
sections.body: A Safe Work Method Statement (SWMS) sets out a particular job and its controls. Proposed illustrated SWMS support would use the actual task, conditions, hazards, controls and approved wording for that work. A general workshop poster has a broader communication role. Both can use humour, with the useful message clear and the job-specific details kept accurate.
bullets: Identify the procedure, task and intended readers.
Get the operational details from the people responsible for the work.
Check the illustration against the reviewed wording.
Keep the current approved source identifiable.
Review changes in the situation before reusing material.

sections.heading: Make the picture earn its place
sections.body: A joke about a bad habit can become confusing when the picture makes that habit look like the recommended method. Direction of travel, hand position, equipment, distances, labels and who is doing what all affect the meaning.
bullets: Distinguish the bad example and the intended behaviour clearly.
Show recognisable equipment and plausible physical actions.
Check captions against what the picture actually depicts.
Use reviewers who understand the task and setting.

sections.heading: Where the work stands
sections.body: The library contains the original source deck, including unverified safety and medical claims, garbled lettering and some picture-and-caption mismatches. It is an archive of the starting material. Workplace products, reviewed adaptations and site-specific versions are in development.
bullets: No source slide is presented here as approved training or an approved SWMS.
Proposed formats show the direction of the project.
A finished workplace item needs its own factual, visual and site review.

library.title: The whole original pile. All 45 slides.
library.lead: The starting material: big headlines, Australian comic humour, mine life, camp life and everyday rough edges.
library.heroAlt: A visual archive of original Rough as Guts illustrated pages arranged as a browsable collection, with varied subjects and layouts.
library.intro: Daz’s supplied deck lives here in full: 42 original images and three text-only introduction slides. Search a topic, open a slide for readable wording and scene notes, or compare the exact original with its optimised web copy below.

systems.title: Keep the good gag. Give it a proper brief.
systems.lead: A practical way to collect observations, blend ideas, check the useful point and turn them into pictures that say what we mean.
systems.heroAlt: An illustrated workbench with an everyday observation, alternate gag sketches, a clear image brief and a finished comic panel.
systems.intro: AI can produce another picture quickly. Getting the right picture takes a clear idea, useful source material and a few deliberate choices. This workflow gives the people making Rough as Guts a shared way to talk about the work.

sections.heading: Catch the moment
sections.body: Start with something someone saw, did or had to clean up after. Write the observation in ordinary language. Capture where it happened, who was involved, what made it funny and what you wished had happened instead.
bullets: Keep the original observation.
Separate what happened from what you are assuming.
Name the habit or decision at the centre of the joke.
Choose the audience who will recognise it.

sections.heading: Find the useful point
sections.body: Say what the reader should understand or do after seeing the page. Keep it small enough to picture. Where the subject involves health, safety or a formal procedure, identify the relevant source and a person able to review it.
bullets: One main point per image or clearly separated panel.
A visible action the reader can recognise.
A factual source when the subject needs one.
An unresolved question recorded as a question.

sections.heading: Try some Loose Goose angles
sections.body: Luke’s Loose Goose Comedy Engine explores real memories through different comic angles and spoken-performance beats. These prompts draw on its Memory Seed, Comedy Lenses and Beat Score. The picture and panel suggestions below adapt those ideas for Rough as Guts.
bullets: Keep the memory and the riff separate. What happened, what do we remember, and what are we guessing or exaggerating? An unknown detail can stay unknown, including someone else’s motives.
Try another angle on the same moment: an observation, a short exchange, acting it out, or telling the joke on yourself. Which version gives us something to explore?
Try a status reversal. Who appears to be in charge or knows what they’re doing? What could happen that changes that impression?
Look for a visual reveal. Could a prop, receipt, picture or expression carry the joke? What happens if we leave the explanation out?

Play with the sequence: setup, turn, punchline, pause and a possible callback. For a comic, could moving the reveal to the next panel change how it reads? For a skit, what happens when we read it aloud?

sections.heading: Write the image before generating it
sections.body: Describe the picture in concrete terms: who is present, what each person is doing, where the action happens and which props matter. State the reading order for panels and make the important action easy to see.
bullets: Specify character variety without requiring one lead character across every edition.
Describe body position, gaze, hands and object placement where they affect meaning.
Give each panel its own scene and purpose.
Set aside clear space for captions and labels.
List visual mistakes that would change the meaning.

sections.heading: Review the result against the brief
sections.body: Look at the image before letting the joke carry you away. Check the action, equipment, expressions, panel sequence and relationship between words and picture. A funny illustration can still communicate the wrong thing.
bullets: Can a reader tell what is happening without an explanation?
Does the picture show the intended action and consequence?
Are important objects, hands and directions plausible?
Does every caption match its panel?
Has any invented lettering or detail changed the point?
Does it suit the audience and setting?

sections.heading: Keep the version worth reusing
sections.body: Save the observation, chosen copy, image brief, references, review notes and finished asset together. When adapting it for a poster, book page or animation, check that the central point still survives. A smaller format may need a simpler idea.
bullets: Record the source and the changes made.
Give each version a clear status.
Keep unresolved review points visible.
Recheck the adapted format before calling it finished.

sections.heading: More clue. Better results.
sections.body: The underlying aim is greater competence: noticing more, understanding the situation and choosing an action that works. A laugh can make that conversation easier. The useful habit is what people take away.

brief_fields.label: Audience
brief_fields.hint: Who should recognise themselves in this?

brief_fields.label: Situation
brief_fields.hint: Where are we, and what has just happened?
brief_fields.example: Someone has cooked dinner and left every pan beside the sink.

brief_fields.label: Useful point
brief_fields.hint: What is the one thing the reader should take away?
brief_fields.example: Cleaning up is part of finishing the meal.

brief_fields.label: Gag
brief_fields.example: The cook declares the job complete while the kitchen looks like a disaster exhibit.

brief_fields.label: Visible action
brief_fields.hint: Describe what each person is doing.
brief_fields.example: The cook presents one plate proudly; a housemate surveys the pile of used pans.

brief_fields.label: Characters and setting
brief_fields.hint: Include only details that help the story.
brief_fields.example: Two adults, ordinary shared kitchen, evening, everyday clothes.

brief_fields.label: Format
brief_fields.hint: Choose a single picture, ordered panels or a short sequence.
brief_fields.example: One wide comic panel with clear space below for a caption.

brief_fields.label: Exact words
brief_fields.hint: Separate the title, caption and any speech.
brief_fields.example: Caption: Dinner is ready. The kitchen has requested backup.

brief_fields.label: Must show / avoid
brief_fields.hint: Name the details that would change the meaning.
brief_fields.example: Show used cookware clearly; avoid making the housemate responsible for cleaning it all.

brief_fields.label: Source and review
brief_fields.hint: What supports the useful point, and what still needs checking?
brief_fields.example: Everyday etiquette concept; review tone with intended readers.

sitemap.title: The whole place, minus the wandering around.
sitemap.lead: Browse the audiences, explore the source material or see how an idea becomes a useful picture.
sitemap.heroAlt: A playful illustrated signpost pointing toward adult guides, Young Crew, workplace material and the source library.
sitemap.intro: Choose an edition, browse Daz’s complete original deck, shape a new image brief in Systems or explore the formats and country wildcards in the Product pipeline.

pipeline.eyebrow: THE ROUGH AS GUTS PRODUCT SHED
pipeline.title: A book is one way out of the shed.
pipeline.lead: A cartoon, a sticker, a skit, a club mascot or something stuck to the back of a dunny door. Possible formats and example jokes to kick around.
pipeline.heroAlt: Four fictional adults develop and display wordless galah comic books, posters, storyboards, stickers, a cap and T-shirts at a country-show creative stall.
pipeline.intro: Books, posters, newsletters, guides and animation were among Luke and Daz's ideas. The concepts below are brainstorm examples, with other directions added for discussion.

products.name: Gift picture books
products.seed: Someone you love treats every household job as an optional side quest.
products.example: The Museum of Things I'll Fix: a guided tour of temporary repairs that have become family heirlooms. Each spread introduces another magnificent exhibit and the person defending it.
products.buyer_or_place: Gift-shop, bookshop, club stall, roadhouse shelf or direct-order edition.
products.next_step: A cover and three illustrated spreads from The Museum of Things I'll Fix.

products.name: Small guides for very specific disasters
products.format: Pocket booklets, zines and fold-out guides
products.seed: A character leaves home and discovers a few jobs that used to happen without their involvement.
products.example: Your First Week Feeding Yourself: a character discovers that a cupboard full of sauces is a recipe for owning sauces. One spread follows a meal from shopping list to the final washing-up.
products.buyer_or_place: Gift packs, local shops, camp welcome packs, library activities or leaving-home presents.
products.next_step: A folded booklet following one meal from an empty fridge to the washing-up.

products.name: The fridge has lodged a complaint
products.seed: The shared fridge is full, nobody owns the smell and everybody owns the good milk.
products.example: A mock statement from the fridge: 'I can keep it cold. I can't make it yours.' A cutaway scene shows labelled lunch boxes, a mystery tub and a worker trying to deny a very familiar casserole dish.
products.buyer_or_place: Camp noticeboards, club kitchens, lunchrooms, sheds and community halls.
products.next_step: A shared-fridge poster with labelled lunch boxes, a mystery tub and the fridge's written complaint.

products.name: The Crib Room Correspondent
products.format: Newsletter column and recurring email feature
products.seed: An everyday object gets a right of reply.
products.example: The kettle writes to management about being left empty. Next issue, the broom responds to allegations that it has never been seen during a shift.
products.buyer_or_place: Club, workplace, camp, association or community newsletters.
products.next_step: An illustrated letter from the kettle, followed by a reply from the broom in the next issue.

products.name: The Rough as Guts Quarterly
products.format: Magazine, seasonal annual or mini newspaper
products.seed: A collection mixing cartoons, fictional letters, puzzles and illustrated stories.
products.example: One issue could contain a shed cartoon, a camp-life letter, a 'spot the pointless extra step' puzzle, a character interview and the Lost Property Awards.
products.buyer_or_place: Local-shop counters, club reading piles, ag-show stalls or a subscription edition.
products.next_step: A sample issue with a shed cartoon, a camp-life letter, a puzzle and the Lost Property Awards.

products.name: Bush Telegraph Toons
products.format: Single-panel newspaper cartoons and four-panel strips
products.seed: A small-town inconvenience becomes an absurd public institution.
products.example: A pothole gets its own office, waiting room and retirement plaque while the road crew tries to find its original job number. The subject is bureaucracy, with room for a different local gripe each week.
products.buyer_or_place: Country newspapers, community news sheets, town newsletters and local websites.
products.next_step: A single-panel pothole cartoon and a four-panel strip about its retirement ceremony.

products.name: The Short Yarn Department
products.format: Caption jokes, illustrated one-liners and share cards
products.seed: An elaborate explanation for an obviously avoidable mess.
products.example: A worker presents an elaborate diagram of where the missing broom could be. Behind him, it is holding the door open.
products.buyer_or_place: Newsletter fillers, club screens, social feeds, calendars and printed cards.
products.next_step: An illustrated broom joke with alternative captions on separate cards.

products.name: The Five-Minute Job
products.format: Comedy sketches, short scripts and performed video
products.seed: A tiny repair attracts a committee and turns into a major operation.
products.example: Two mates begin with a loose cupboard handle. Each helpful arrival brings a larger tool and a longer explanation. The quiet person who fetched the right screw finishes the job while the committee is still discussing access.
products.buyer_or_place: Hall gigs, club nights, short video series and camp entertainment.
products.next_step: A short script for the cupboard-handle repair, with entrances for each increasingly helpful visitor.

products.name: Small signs with a point
products.format: Sticker sheets, labels, magnets and removable decals
products.seed: A small joke attached to the cupboard, appliance or lunch box involved.
products.example: A dishwasher sticker reads 'A cupboard with consequences' above a tiny character carefully stacking a plate. A shared-food label says 'This has an owner. Apparently that's me.'
products.buyer_or_place: Club kitchens, households, lunch boxes, sheds, welcome packs and gift bundles.
products.next_step: A sheet of dishwasher, lunch-box and shared-fridge labels with small character illustrations.

products.name: Illustrated support for the actual SWMS
products.format: Task drawings and visual companions to reviewed safe work method statements
products.seed: Illustrations of a specific task, linked to its written sequence and actual equipment.
products.example: A matching task sheet drawn from the equipment, location and sequence in a supplied, reviewed SWMS. The responsible task team checks the depicted controls and steps before using it in their material.
products.buyer_or_place: Task-specific work documents and site training material, with the responsible organisation and reviewers.
products.next_step: A task drawing beside its supplied SWMS, with source details and reviewer notes.
products.review_note: Safe Work Australia's guidance describes SWMS for high risk construction work. This proposal is illustration support tied to the specific work and its review process.

products.name: When the job is “finished”
products.format: Short animation, loops and recurring episodes
products.seed: Someone declares a job finished while the part they dislike is left for somebody else.
products.example: Possible scene: the cook announces “Dinner’s done” over one plate and every saucepan in the house. Would the reveal carry the joke, or does it need a reply from the person facing the washing-up?
products.buyer_or_place: Short-video channels, club screens, event displays and companion content for books.
products.next_step: Try a silent reveal of the kitchen, then a version with the reply “You missed a bit.” Compare whether the joke is clear and whether either version feels like a familiar household moment.

products.name: Objects that carry the joke
products.format: Tea towels, mugs, aprons, shirts, calendars and shed prints
products.seed: A useful household object comments on the job it keeps being denied.
products.example: A tea towel shows the Workload Forecast: dishes gathering over the sink, clearing after someone actually dries them. An apron gives the cook a dramatic title beside a very modest meal.
products.buyer_or_place: Gift stalls, club fundraisers, roadhouses, small shops and direct-order bundles.
products.next_step: A Workload Forecast tea towel mock-up, with a matching sink-side print.

products.name: Give the club a larrikin
products.format: Sports-club mascots, match-day cartoons and junior activity sheets
products.seed: A fictional club character who can call a mark across the oval and miss the roster on the wall.
products.example: A fictional galah mascot announces itself as Head of Encouragement and Avoiding the Washing-Up. It can star in a match-day strip, a volunteer thank-you, a gear-return reminder and a junior colouring page.
products.buyer_or_place: Footy, cricket, bowls and other sports clubs, with a character developed for the individual club.
products.next_step: An original galah character sheet, a match-day cartoon and a gear-return notice.

products.name: Political campaigns & public-issue cartoons
products.format: Generic public-facing issue cartoons, campaign posters and explainer strips
products.seed: An ordinary public problem is buried under grand language and an unhelpful process.
products.example: Shed Parliament debates who left the gate open while a goat eats the minutes. A separate factual panel explains the relevant public process using checked, clearly sourced information.
products.buyer_or_place: Public exhibitions, community papers, civic information projects and issue-based public campaigns.
products.next_step: A Shed Parliament cartoon paired with a sourced explanation of a specific public process.
products.scope: General public-facing issues and satire. Concepts are not tailored to demographic groups or voter profiles.

products.name: Next week on the noticeboard
products.format: Serial comic panels and rotating community displays
products.seed: A character's unfinished job keeps acquiring new consequences.
products.example: A lost property box begins as one lonely glove. Each instalment gives it a new resident, a new rule and eventually a committee demanding a larger box.
products.buyer_or_place: Camp noticeboards, halls, club foyers, libraries and community shops.
products.next_step: A sequence of noticeboard panels following the lost property box from lonely glove to overcrowded institution.

products.name: A yarn, a picture and a room full of mates
products.format: Illustrated readings, hall-night comedy and caption contests
products.seed: A narrated picture about a familiar habit, with room for competing explanations.
products.example: A silent picture of a wildly overpacked ute, accompanied by increasingly confident explanations and a final reveal of the one thing its owner forgot.
products.buyer_or_place: Country halls, bowls clubs, show events, libraries and informal club entertainment.
products.next_step: A short illustrated reading with an overpacked-ute picture, competing explanations and a final reveal.

products.name: “Just a quick favour”
products.format: Short audio yarns, radio-ready sketches and narrated cartoons
products.seed: A request to pick up a couple of things grows until it sounds like a house move.
products.example: Possible phone sketch: a mate asks to borrow the ute, then keeps adding furniture to the list. The other person asks, “Am I helping you move, or do I live with you now?” Does the growing request offer enough to play with?
products.buyer_or_place: Community-radio submissions, club audio, podcasts and accessible narrated editions.
products.next_step: Read it aloud with the requests delivered casually, then with increasingly obvious attempts to hide the scale of the favour. Which version, if either, gives the other person a useful comic response?

products.name: The Smoko Argument Pack
products.format: Caption games, scenario cards and printable club activities
products.seed: Players supply the excuse a character might give for an obvious mess.
products.example: One card shows a ute packed for a ten-minute errand. Players supply the missing explanation, predict the forgotten item or match it to the worst possible tool.
products.buyer_or_place: Club tables, family gatherings, camp recreation rooms and gift packs.
products.next_step: A printable pack of picture cards, excuse cards and a one-page set of game rules.

wildcards.title: The Cubicle Gazette
wildcards.setting: Country-show toilets, club bathrooms and camp amenities, with permission from the venue.
wildcards.idea: A tiny changing newspaper for the back of the door, complete with a headline, one cartoon and an absurd classified ad.
wildcards.visual: A serious broadsheet front page reporting that the last clean mug has been sighted near the sink.
wildcards.pilot: A door-sized newspaper sheet with one cartoon, a mock headline and a classified ad.

wildcards.title: The Lost Property Royal Show
wildcards.setting: An ag-show display or club foyer.
wildcards.idea: Abandoned everyday objects receive the treatment of prize livestock, complete with judging notes and ribbons.
wildcards.visual: A magnificent unmatched glove under a Champion ribbon; a line of hopeful coffee mugs waits to be judged.
wildcards.pilot: Removable illustrated award cards and a miniature display of fictional prize-winning lost property.

wildcards.title: The Corrugated Comic
wildcards.setting: A show stand, shed exhibition or temporary community-art display.
wildcards.idea: A comic designed across a series of upright corrugated panels, so readers walk along the story.
wildcards.visual: A three-stage attempt to close a stubborn gate, ending with the quiet discovery that somebody stacked timber behind it.
wildcards.pilot: A paper model of the comic wall and a sample illustrated panel.

wildcards.title: Moppa's Feral Chores Club
wildcards.setting: A family activity day, junior club session or illustrated home edition.
wildcards.idea: A proudly scruffy emu becomes an accidental ambassador for finishing jobs.
wildcards.visual: Moppa insists a mess is a creative project while sweeping it into the unmistakable shape of a second emu.
wildcards.pilot: A character sheet, a short strip and a chores activity page.

wildcards.title: The Roadhouse Placemat Yarn
wildcards.idea: A one-meal comic, caption puzzle or small 'spot the forgotten item' scene that can be read while food arrives.
wildcards.visual: A traveller packed everything for the trip except the reason they stopped: the shopping list still pinned to the fridge at home.
wildcards.pilot: A paper placemat with a comic and a missing-item puzzle arranged around the plate space.

wildcards.title: The Shed Choir
wildcards.setting: A hall gig or club variety night.
wildcards.idea: A performed comedy piece builds a familiar shed soundtrack from voices, ordinary props and increasingly unhelpful commentary.
wildcards.visual: Solemn performers hold caption cards while one person supplies a tool noise and another disputes its accuracy.
wildcards.pilot: A short script, caption cards and an audio demo of the shed soundtrack.

wildcards.title: The Town's Unofficial Useful Map
wildcards.setting: A fictional town in a book, show display or local publication concept.
wildcards.idea: A fictional town mapped through unofficial landmarks: a shady seat, an awkward shop door and the bend where the recurring visitor takes the wrong turn.
wildcards.visual: A friendly illustrated town map with character vignettes and a recurring visitor getting increasingly overconfident.
wildcards.pilot: An illustrated map of a fictional town, with its unofficial landmarks and recurring visitors.

routes.title: The shared fridge
steps: Poster: a cutaway fridge giving evidence about an ownerless casserole and somebody else's missing milk.
Crib-room column: a letter from the fridge requesting that its occupants stop referring to the smell as 'a maintenance issue'.
Thirty-second skit: workers disown a mystery tub until somebody announces that the container is free to take home.
routes.note: One situation with a visual version, a written voice and a performed exchange.

routes.title: The club galah
steps: Match-day cartoon: the galah loudly coaches from the boundary while facing the wrong oval.
Gear-return notice: the same galah beside a mountain of club equipment and an empty bag labelled with its name.
Merchandise: a cap or shirt showing the galah as 'Head of Encouragement and Avoiding the Washing-Up'.
routes.note: The same fictional character in a cartoon, a club notice and a wearable joke.
